**Video:** [Lec 40 — SVM with Kernel Function](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dDIutyWTPKA)

## Learning goals

- Lift data with $\phi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d'}$ so a **linear** SVM in feature space yields a nonlinear rule in $x$.
- Replace $\phi(x_i)^\top\phi(x_j)$ by a **kernel** $K(x_i,x_j)$ (kernel trick).
- Name common kernels (polynomial, Gaussian / RBF) and the historical handoff to neural nets.

## Before this clicks

Dual SVM objectives depend on data only through inner products $x_i^\top x_j$. If you replace $x$ by $\phi(x)$, you only need $\phi(x_i)^\top\phi(x_j)$. A kernel computes that inner product **without building $\phi(x)$ explicitly**. Soft-margin still applies in feature space if points remain inseparable after the lift.

---

## Main ideas

### 1. Feature maps

Choose $\phi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d'}$ with $d'\gg d$ (sometimes infinite). Linear separator in $\phi$-space:

$$
f(x)=w^\top\phi(x)+b
$$

can be a highly nonlinear function of the original $x$ (same spirit as generalized linear regression with basis features). Separability becomes “more plausible,” not guaranteed.

### 2. Dual with features

The dual quadratic term becomes

$$
\mu_i\mu_j y_i y_j\,\phi(x_i)^\top\phi(x_j).
$$

### 3. Kernel function and kernel trick

A **kernel** $K:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfies

$$
K(x,x')=\phi(x)^\top\phi(x')
$$

for some feature map $\phi$ (Mercer / PSD Gram matrix conditions in the background).

**Kernel trick:** wherever the algorithm needs an inner product in $\phi$-space, write $K(x,x')$ and stay in the original coordinates. You never instantiate $\phi(x)$ if $K$ is cheap.

Examples:

| Kernel | Form (schematic) | Feature intuition |
|--------|------------------|-------------------|
| Linear | $x^\top x'$ | $\phi=\mathrm{id}$ |
| Polynomial | $(x^\top x'+c)^{p}$ | monomials up to degree $p$ |
| Gaussian / RBF | $\exp(-\|x-x'\|^2/(2\sigma^{2}))$ | infinite-dimensional lift |

RBF decision surfaces resemble RBF-network style expansions; class notes the kinship without equating the whole models.

### 4. Decision rule

With $w=\sum_i\mu_i y_i\phi(x_i)$,

$$
f(x)=\sum_{i\in\mathrm{SV}}\mu_i y_i K(x_i,x)+b.
$$

Only support vectors enter the sum.

### 5. Historical moral

Large margins yield clean generalization stories; late-1990s SVMs were SOTA. At modern scale / raw high-dimensional perception, “project until linearly separable” is not guaranteed, and kernels struggle vs representation learning. Course now moves to **neural networks** (universal approximation, backprop, then CNN/RNN/Transformers), with trees/ensembles later.

---

## Worked mini-example

XOR-like four points in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ are not linearly separable. With $\phi(x)=(x_1,x_2,x_1 x_2)$ (or a suitable polynomial kernel), a linear SVM in $\phi$-space separates them; the boundary in $x$-space is curved. Practically you call $K$ instead of building $\phi$.

---

## Common confusions

| Confusion | Clarification |
|-----------|---------------|
| Kernel = neural net activation | Kernel is an **inner-product shortcut** in a feature space. |
| Must know $\phi$ explicitly | Only $K$ is required for training/prediction. |
| Kernel SVM solved all of ML | Scaling and representation issues returned the crown to nets. |

## Self-check questions

1. Why map $x\mapsto\phi(x)$ before a linear SVM?
2. What identity defines a kernel $K$ relative to $\phi$?
3. State the kernel trick in one sentence.
4. Write the Gaussian / RBF kernel.
5. Express $f(x)$ using $K$ and support vectors.
